groups.title: Verses some Bibles leave out
groups.intro: These verses are in the KJV. Bibles translated from the oldest manuscripts (the ASV, BBE and most modern versions) leave them out or put them in a footnote, because those manuscripts don't have them. Most scholars think copyists added them, often from a parallel passage; some hold that the oldest copies dropped them.

groups.title: Passages the Bibles here split on
groups.intro: The KJV prints all of these; the other Bibles differ. They are missing from some of the oldest manuscripts, so modern editions often set them in brackets or add a note.

groups.title: Moved, not missing
groups.intro: Sometimes the words are all there, but in a different place.

items.note: “This kind goes out only by prayer and fasting” is not in Codex Sinaiticus (first hand) or Codex Vaticanus. It matches Mark 9:29, and copyists likely added it here from there.

kjv.t: Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting.

web.t: But this kind doesn’t go out except by prayer and fasting.”

items.note: Not in Sinaiticus or Vaticanus. The words echo Luke 19:10 (“the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost”).

kjv.t: For the Son of man is come to save that which was lost.

web.t: For the Son of Man came to save that which was lost.

items.note: Not in Sinaiticus or Vaticanus. The same saying about devouring widows’ houses is in Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47; manuscripts that have it here don’t agree where to put it (before or after verse 13).

kjv.t: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows’ houses, and for a pretence make long prayer: therefore ye shall receive the greater damnation.

web.t: “But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! Because you shut up the Kingdom of Heaven against men; for you don’t enter in yourselves, neither do you allow those who are entering in to enter.

items.note: “If any man have ears to hear, let him hear” is not in Sinaiticus or Vaticanus; it repeats Mark 4:9 and 4:23.

kjv.t: If any man have ears to hear, let him hear.

web.t: If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear!”

items.note: Verses 44 and 46 repeat verse 48 word for word (“where their worm dieth not…”). They are not in Sinaiticus or Vaticanus.

kjv.t: Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.

web.t: ‘where their worm doesn’t die, and the fire is not quenched.’

items.note: Same as verse 44: a repeat of verse 48, not in Sinaiticus or Vaticanus.

kjv.t: Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.

web.t: ‘where their worm doesn’t die, and the fire is not quenched.’

items.note: Not in Sinaiticus or Vaticanus. It matches Matthew 6:15 (“if ye forgive not… neither will your Father forgive”).

kjv.t: But if ye do not forgive, neither will your Father which is in heaven forgive your trespasses.

web.t: But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father in heaven forgive your transgressions.”

items.note: “He was numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12) is not in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus or Vaticanus; Luke 22:37 quotes the same line.

kjv.t: And the scripture was fulfilled, which saith, And he was numbered with the transgressors.

web.t: The Scripture was fulfilled which says, “He was counted with transgressors.”

items.note: “Two men shall be in the field…” is in few Greek manuscripts (it is missing from most, which is why the WEB leaves it out too); it matches Matthew 24:40.

kjv.t: Two men shall be in the field; the one shall be taken, and the other left.

items.note: The custom of releasing a prisoner at the feast is not in some of the oldest manuscripts (the papyrus P75, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus); Matthew 27:15 and Mark 15:6 tell of it.

kjv.t: (For of necessity he must release one unto them at the feast.)

web.t: Now he had to release one prisoner to them at the feast.

items.note: The angel who stirred the water of the pool (with the end of verse 3, “waiting for the moving of the water”) is not in the oldest manuscripts (the papyri P66 and P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus). It reads like an explanation of verse 7 that entered the text.

kjv.t: For an angel went down at a certain season into the pool, and troubled the water: whosoever then first after the troubling of the water stepped in was made whole of whatsoever disease he had.

web.t: for an angel went down at certain times into the pool and stirred up the water. Whoever stepped in first after the stirring of the water was healed of whatever disease he had.

items.note: The eunuch’s confession (“I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God”) is in few Greek manuscripts but in Latin ones; Erasmus included it in his Greek New Testament, and so it came into the KJV. Most Greek manuscripts don’t have it, so the WEB leaves it out too.

kjv.t: And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.

items.note: “It pleased Silas to abide there still” is missing from most Greek manuscripts (so the WEB leaves it out too). It may have been added to explain why Silas is still in Antioch in verse 40.

kjv.t: Notwithstanding it pleased Silas to abide there still.

items.note: The end of verse 6, verse 7 and the start of verse 8 (Lysias taking Paul away by force) are missing from most Greek manuscripts, so the WEB leaves them out too.

kjv.t: But the chief captain Lysias came upon us, and with great violence took him away out of our hands,

items.note: “The Jews departed, and had great reasoning among themselves” is not in the oldest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus).

kjv.t: And when he had said these words, the Jews departed, and had great reasoning among themselves.

web.t: When he had said these words, the Jews departed, having a great dispute among themselves.

items.note: This blessing (“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all”) repeats verse 20 and is not in the oldest manuscripts.

kjv.t: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.

web.t: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all! Amen.

items.note: The “longer ending” of Mark. Sinaiticus and Vaticanus end the Gospel at 16:8, with the women afraid; one Latin manuscript has a short ending instead, and a few have both. Early writers (Eusebius, Jerome) knew of copies without it. Most later manuscripts include verses 9–20.

kjv.t: Now when Jesus was risen early the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, out of whom he had cast seven devils.
And she went and told them that had been with him, as they mourned and wept.
And they, when they had heard that he was alive, and had been seen of her, believed not.

web.t: Now when he had risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons.
She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept.
When they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they disbelieved.

asv.t: Now when he was risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons.
She went and told them that had been with him, as they mourned and wept.
And they, when they heard that he was alive, and had been seen of her, disbelieved.

items.note: The woman taken in adultery (7:53–8:11) is not in the oldest manuscripts (P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus). In later manuscripts it appears here, or after John 7:36, 21:25 or Luke 21:38. Many think it is an old story about Jesus that was kept outside the Gospels at first.

kjv.t: And every man went unto his own house.

web.t: Everyone went to his own house,

asv.t: And they went every man unto his own house:

items.note: The words “in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one. And there are three that bear witness in earth” (the Johannine Comma) come from Latin manuscripts. Only a handful of late Greek manuscripts have them; Erasmus added them in his third edition (1522), and so they are in the KJV. The WEB and ASV don’t have them. (The ASV numbers these verses a little differently, so its verse 7 begins with words the KJV has in verse 6.)

kjv.t: For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.
And there are three that bear witness in earth, the Spirit, and the water, and the blood: and these three agree in one.

web.t: For there are three who testify:
the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and the three agree as one.

asv.t: And it is the Spirit that beareth witness, because the Spirit is the truth.
For there are three who bear witness, the Spirit, and the water, and the blood: and the three agree in one.

items.note: The end of the Lord’s Prayer, “For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen,” is not in Sinaiticus or Vaticanus, and Luke’s version (Luke 11:2–4) doesn’t have it. A similar closing is in the Didache, an early Christian manual. The KJV and WEB have it; the ASV doesn’t.

kjv.t: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.

web.t: Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.’

asv.t: And bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.

items.note: The angel strengthening Jesus and his sweat “as it were great drops of blood” are missing from some of the oldest manuscripts (P75, Vaticanus) but present in others (Sinaiticus, the first hand). Editors disagree; all the Bibles here print the verses.

kjv.t: And there appeared an angel unto him from heaven, strengthening him.
And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground.

web.t: An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him.
Being in agony, he prayed more earnestly. His sweat became like great drops of blood falling down on the ground.

asv.t: And there appeared unto him an angel from heaven, strengthening him.
And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became as it were great drops of blood falling down upon the ground.

items.note: The closing praise (“Now to him that is of power to stablish you…”) ends chapter 16 in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and the KJV (the oldest papyrus, P46, has it after chapter 15), but stands at the end of chapter 14 in most later manuscripts, so the WEB prints it as Romans 14:24–26.

kjv.t: Now to him that is of power to stablish you according to my gospel, and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery, which was kept secret since the world began,
But now is made manifest, and by the scriptures of the prophets, according to the commandment of the everlasting God, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith:
To God only wise, be glory through Jesus Christ for ever. Amen.

asv.t: Now to him that is able to establish you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery which hath been kept in silence through times eternal,
but now is manifested, and by the scriptures of the prophets, according to the commandment of the eternal God, is made known unto all the nations unto obedience of faith:
to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory for ever. Amen.
